extracted.intended_audience: educated general readership; aspiring critics, readers of The Spectator, and those interested in literary taste and social manners
extracted.subtask_description: Short prescriptive essays on what makes a good literary critic and on proper decency, liberality, charity, fortune, and marital economy — offering evaluative standards for critics' conduct and for social virtues. Advice is phrased as norms and illustrated with classical and contemporary examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of a good critic
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic must have taste and learning, the ability to think right, and the skill to convey thoughts with clearness and perspicuity; he should be a master of the elegance and delicacy of his native tongue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by appeal to Aristotle as both best critic and logician; an author who cannot distinguish between words and things or range his thoughts will be confused and obscure. Greek and Latin critics demonstrate that critical style itself evidences mastery of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish words from things and arrange thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics (and writers) must learn the art of distinguishing between words and things and of ranging their thoughts and setting them in proper lights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without this skill, even correct notions become lost in confusion and obscurity; Locke's Essay is an odd book for a would-be critic, but the underlying point is that clarity of thought and expression is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide learning across arts and sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: A true critic should have insight into all the parts of learning; lacking acquaintance with ordinary systems of arts and sciences marks an unlearned critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many English writers who try to be critics reveal by their phrases and confused thinking that they lack common systems of knowledge; relying on a few French rules and cant can set up an illiterate writer as a critic, which is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial or fashionable rules (anti-cant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute a few general rules or a cant of words (e.g., imported French rules) for genuine taste and learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such general rules can enable an illiterate heavy writer to appear judicious; beware of mere formulaic criticism that masks ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise excellencies rather than dwell on small faults
rubrics_metrics.description: A true critic ought to dwell upon excellencies rather than imperfections and to discover concealed beauties of a writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics who only venture to praise passages already applauded by the public and turn wholly upon little faults are easily successful but poor judges; the public and 'rabble' are apt to laugh at anything witty, which can make ridicule mistaken for judgment (Dryden's lines quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attack 'glowing bold expressions' by ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: It is easy to fix a mark upon a 'verbum ardens' (a glowing bold expression) and turn it into ridicule; this is a sign of crude criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tully's observation shows that a cold ill-natured criticism can make beauties seem ridiculous; a little wit can expose a beauty as well as a fault, so the critic who lacks taste will unjustly attack fine strokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using wit or ridicule in improper places
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit shown in an improper place is impertinent and absurd; critics should not use the gift of ridicule as a means to attack passages merely because they furnish an opportunity for merriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such pleasantry prejudices the reader rather than convinces him; the greatest masters of criticism appear with a serious and instructive air, and ridicule is unfair and disingenuous in works of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize discovery and communication of what is worth observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic's duty is to communicate to the world such things as are worth their observation, revealing concealed beauties and the most exquisite words and strokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should make readers notice merits they might otherwise miss; the 'sower undistinguishing Critick' who attacks delicate passages fails in this duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper in criticizing great genius
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticising a great genius (e.g., Milton), point at imperfections without endeavouring to inflame them with ridicule; works of great genius with many lapses are preferable to the exact works of inferior authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premise offered before critique of Paradise Lost: enter upon the ungrateful work of pointing out imperfections but without ridicule; Longinus noted that productions of great genius are infinitely preferable though they have lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bestow favours and liberality with decency and cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality should be performed with such cheerfulness as to express the god-like pleasure of obliging fellow-creatures; manner in bestowing doubles the kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pliny's letter offering substantial help done in a pleasing, unassuming way; contrast Mummius (consenting in a manner that makes the benefaction lose its name) with Carus (whose manner doubles the kindness). Gifts should out-run the receiver's wishes and not appear grudging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency is necessary handmaid to virtue and religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue without decency can appear sour and ill-humoured; decency as accompaniment makes religion and other virtues attractive and lovely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decency adds comeliness to religion and gives the just title to the beauty of holiness; without it, valour degenerates into brutality, learning into pedantry, genteel demeanour into affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comeliness and decorum increase persuasive force
rubrics_metrics.description: Comeliness of person and decency of behaviour add infinite weight to what is pronounced by one; a graceful and becoming severity makes rebuke more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Milton's description where a beauteous angel's grave rebuke abashed the Devil; decorum can make advice or rebuke have effect where rigid severity fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve decency even in death
rubrics_metrics.description: Great minds preserved decent posture and behaviour up to their last moments; the manner of dying can be an expression of decorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Caesar gathered his robe about him to avoid falling unbecomingly; Lucretia's last concern was that her body should lie in an attitude worthy of the mind which had inhabited it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge the role of fortune; avoid attributing success solely to prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is presumptuous to ascribe successes entirely to our own management; one should regard many successes as the bounty of Heaven and not boast of prudence alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and arguments: Queen Elizabeth's medal credits God for scattering the Armada; anecdotes about generals noting fortune's role; arrogance and conceitedness about abilities are offensive and may be punished by fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance prudence and boldness when seeking success
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence, with its caution, may hinder extraordinary success that sometimes comes from rashness or a sanguine temper; therefore prudence is not a guarantee of great fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The race is not always to the swift; great unforeseen events can pervert the best-laid schemes; young people may be favoured by fortune over the cautious old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wealth to exert benevolence; failure to help the poor is insolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper use of riches implies a man should exert all good qualities — justice, beneficence, charity — and being rich without mindful help to the poor is monstrous and insolent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of wealthy who support pomp and luxury but neglect the needy; charity-schools praised as laudable institutions that produce useful servants and public benefit; suggested concrete acts (e.g., donating birthday silk value to charity-school).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for worthy benefaction (charity-schools)
rubrics_metrics.description: A worthy benefaction is done without expectation of return, for public good, and especially for infants who will become honest artisans; charity yields civil and religious improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charity-schools supply learning 'without money, and without price' and are more edifying for the poor; benefits include producing humble, grateful servants and preventing domestic slanders born of poor upbringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage economics: separate purses are unnatural
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate purses between husband and wife are as unnatural as separate beds; marriage cannot be happy where pleasures, inclinations, and interests of both parties are not the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of the late practice of 'pin-money' as furnishing a woman with arms against her husband and as setting up a retreat plan; separate allowances suggest distrust and may be 'penny wise and pound foolish.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Pin-money as a sign of distrust and a bad marital precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The insistence on pin-money is viewed as extraordinary, a precaution for retreat, and an accessory to a husband's dishonour; it is a late custom unknown to ancestors and improper to encourage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: it encourages separate interests, may be requested in excessive sums, and implies planning for separation rather than unified domestic life; separate allowances are likened to leaving a secured retreat in battle.
